lesson.title: Cahokia and the Mound Builders of the Mississippi Valley
lesson.summary: This section examines the Mississippian culture, a network of farming societies across the American Southeast and Midwest known for large earthen mounds, extensive trade, and the city of Cahokia, the largest urban center north of Mexico before European contact.
lesson.body:
Beginning roughly around 800 CE and continuing for several centuries, a distinctive way of life spread across river valleys of the American Southeast and Midwest, one that archaeologists call the Mississippian culture. It was not a single nation or government but a shared set of practices: intensive maize agriculture, large earthen platform mounds used as bases for temples and elite residences, and a related set of religious symbols and artifacts, all spreading among many different peoples connected by trade and cultural exchange along the Mississippi River and its tributaries. This culture emerged from the same agricultural foundation, corn farming supplemented by beans and squash, that had transformed North American societies more broadly.

The greatest Mississippian city was Cahokia, located near present day St. Louis, Missouri, at the confluence of the Mississippi, Missouri, and Illinois Rivers. At its peak, around 1050 to 1200 CE, Cahokia's population likely reached into the thousands, with some estimates suggesting it may have grown considerably larger, making it the largest city north of Mexico at the time and comparable in scale to some contemporary European cities. Its skyline was dominated by Monks Mound, an enormous earthen platform roughly one hundred feet tall, built entirely through human labor carrying basket loads of soil, atop which stood a large wooden structure believed to be a temple or the residence of a paramount chief.

Cahokia and other Mississippian centers were not isolated. Archaeologists have found copper from the Great Lakes region, marine shells from the Gulf of Mexico, and mica from the southern Appalachians at Mississippian sites, evidence of trade networks stretching across much of the continent. Sites across this network also share a common set of symbols, including motifs like the falcon warrior, weeping eye designs, and serpent imagery, that scholars group under the term Southeastern Ceremonial Complex, suggesting that shared religious and political ideas circulated widely among otherwise distinct communities. Games like chunkey, played by rolling a stone disk and throwing spears to predict where it would stop, were popular across the region and appear often in Mississippian art and artifacts.

For reasons still debated by scholars, possibly including resource depletion, climate shifts, warfare, or social and political upheaval, Cahokia declined sharply after about 1200 CE and was largely abandoned by the 1400s, well before sustained European contact. Other Mississippian centers persisted longer, and the societies encountered by early European explorers and colonists in the Southeast, including the ancestors of the Muscogee, Natchez, Choctaw, and Chickasaw peoples, were direct cultural descendants of this Mississippian tradition, even as the great cities of its height had already passed into memory.

Cahokia's rise and fall matters for understanding North American history for a simple reason: it demonstrates that large, complex, urbanized societies existed in what is now the United States centuries before Columbus, and that those societies had their own histories of growth and decline that owed nothing to European contact. When later colonists encountered indigenous societies that seemed, to them, less centralized than Cahokia had been at its height, they were often looking at societies still adapting to the aftermath of Mississippian decline, not evidence of some inherent limitation in Native American civilization.
